content.title: About
content.content: Taffy is a soft, stretchy candy made from sugar, corn syrup, butter, and flavorings. It has a sweet, slightly caramel-like taste and a chewy texture. Taffy is usually sold in small bite‑size pieces, individually wrapped.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Taffy originated in the United States in the early 19th century and quickly became a popular treat.
Traditionally, taffy is pulled by hand, creating its characteristic fibrous structure.
Different countries have their own names: in the UK it’s often called “taffy,” in Japan “karēmu.”
Taffy is frequently used as an ingredient in desserts, ice cream, and baked goods.
There are many flavor variations: classic vanilla, strawberry, mint, sea‑salt caramel, and more.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The sugar in taffy is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate boost of glucose.

items.title: Contains a small amount of fat
items.content: Butter adds a modest amount of saturated fat, which can be part of a balanced diet in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Some recipes are fortified with vitamins B1, B2, and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise blood glucose levels and contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The soft, stretchy texture can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Taffy can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to ice cream, yogurt, baked goods, or used as a decorative garnish for desserts. Keep it in a dry place to prevent stickiness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store taffy in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent sugar crystallization.
